lines.text: For more than a hundred and sixty million years, reptiles of every size ruled the land. This is the story of the dinosaurs, and of the people who dug them up.
It begins about two hundred and fifty million years ago, with the Mesozoic: the age of reptiles, on land, in the sea and in the air.
Its first chapter is the Triassic. Life was rebuilding after a great extinction, and among the newcomers were the very first dinosaurs.
In the seas swam the ichthyosaurs, shaped like dolphins, breathing air and giving birth to live young.
And on land, a new group of reptiles appeared. They would rule for over a hundred and sixty million years, and one branch of them is still here: the birds.
One of the earliest we know is Eoraptor, a small two-legged animal about a metre long, from what is now Argentina.
Beside it lived Herrerasaurus, an early meat eater that grew up to six metres long.
Coelophysis was slender and fast. Hundreds of its skeletons were found together at Ghost Ranch in New Mexico.
In Triassic Europe, long-necked Plateosaurus ate plants, an early relative of the giants still to come.
Then came the Jurassic. The great continent Pangaea broke apart, the Atlantic began to open, and the giants arrived.
It opened with a mass extinction that wiped out many large reptiles, and cleared the way for dinosaurs to take over.
Plesiosaurs took to the oceans: broad bodies, four flippers and, in many kinds, a very long neck.
On land hunted Dilophosaurus, a large early predator with two thin crests on its head.
Megalosaurus was a meat eater from England. In 1824 it became the first dinosaur ever given a scientific name.
Late in the Jurassic came Stegosaurus, with tall bony plates along its back and spikes on its tail.
Its world belonged to Allosaurus, the top hunter of its time, with a large head and sharp, curved teeth.
Diplodocus was very long indeed, with a slender neck at one end and a tail like a whip at the other.
Brachiosaurus stood differently. Its front legs were longer than its back legs, so its body sloped upward like a giraffe's.
And there was Apatosaurus, another whip-tailed giant, long confused with Brontosaurus.
Then something small and remarkable: Archaeopteryx, the size of a crow, with feathers and wings, but also teeth and a long bony tail.
Compsognathus was no bigger than a turkey, and for many years it was the smallest dinosaur known.
The last chapter is the Cretaceous. Flowering plants spread, the seas were high and warm, and the most famous dinosaurs of all appeared.
In North Africa lived Spinosaurus, a giant with a tall sail on its back and a snout like a crocodile's.
Iguanodon ate plants and carried a spike on each thumb. It was only the second dinosaur ever named.
Sinosauropteryx, found in China in 1996, was the first dinosaur known to have feathers without being a bird.
Deinonychus was fast and feathered, with a large claw on each foot. Its study changed how scientists pictured dinosaurs: active, not slow.
From Argentina came Giganotosaurus, one of the largest meat eaters, as long as Tyrannosaurus or longer.
And Argentinosaurus, among the heaviest animals ever to walk on land. We know it from only a few bones, so its true size is an estimate.
Overhead flew Pteranodon, with a long toothless beak and wings up to seven metres across. A flying reptile, but not a dinosaur.
In the sea, Mosasaurus hunted with powerful jaws. It was a relative of today's lizards and snakes.
Parasaurolophus had a duck's bill and a long hollow crest, which it may have used to make loud calls.
Velociraptor lived in Mongolia. It was feathered and about the size of a turkey, much smaller than the one in the films.
Oviraptor was once thought to steal eggs. Later finds showed it was sitting on its own nest.
Protoceratops was a horned plant eater the size of a sheep. One was found locked in a fight with a Velociraptor.
Stranger still was Therizinosaurus, a plant eater with claws up to a metre long.
Pachycephalosaurus wore a dome of solid bone on its head, as much as twenty-five centimetres thick.
In South America hunted Carnotaurus, with two horns above its eyes and tiny arms.
And then the one everybody knows: Tyrannosaurus rex, with a huge skull and a very strong bite, one of the largest meat eaters ever to walk the land.
It shared its world with Triceratops, a plant eater with a bony frill and three horns on its face.
Ankylosaurus was built like a tank, covered in bony plates, with a club of bone at the end of its tail.
Above them soared Quetzalcoatlus, one of the largest flying animals of all time, with wings as wide as a small aeroplane.
Then, about sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid perhaps ten kilometres wide struck what is now Mexico.
What followed killed about three quarters of all species. The dinosaurs were gone, all except the birds.
Millions of years later, people began to find them. Mary Anning of Lyme Regis pulled the skeletons of sea reptiles from the cliffs of the Dorset coast.
In 1842 the anatomist Richard Owen gave these animals their name: dinosaurs, the terrible lizards.
Soon London had the first life-size dinosaur sculptures in the world. They are still standing in their park today.
In America, two rival fossil hunters, Cope and Marsh, raced each other bitterly, and between them found dozens of new dinosaurs.
In 1990, in South Dakota, came Sue: the largest and most complete Tyrannosaurus skeleton ever found.
And in 1993 a film brought them back to life on screen, and changed how films were made.
The giants are gone, but their story is still being dug out of the ground.
